Nehemiah 1.summary: In the month Chisleu, Nehemiah is at Shushan the palace when Hanani and men of Judah tell him that the remnant are "in great affliction" and the wall of Jerusalem is broken down (Nehemiah 1:1–3). Nehemiah sits down and weeps, mourns, fasts, and prays (Nehemiah 1:4). He praises the God "that keepeth covenant and mercy," confesses the sins of Israel and of his father's house, and recalls God's promise through Moses to gather his people if they return (Nehemiah 1:5–10). He asks for mercy before "this man," for he was the king's cupbearer (Nehemiah 1:11).
Nehemiah 1.whereWeAre: Ezra ended with the people putting away their foreign wives. Some years later, at Shushan the palace, Nehemiah hears that Jerusalem's wall is still broken down, and he weeps, fasts, and prays. In chapter 2 he asks the king to send him there.

keyFigures.name: Nehemiah
keyFigures.role: The king's cupbearer, who weeps, fasts, and prays for Jerusalem.

keyFigures.name: Hanani
keyFigures.role: One of Nehemiah's brethren, who brings news of Jerusalem's broken wall.

keyThemes.explanation: Bad news drives Nehemiah to weep, fast, and pray before he acts.
Nehemiah confesses his own family's sin along with Israel's.
He asks God to keep his word to gather the people who return to him.

Nehemiah 2.summary: In the month Nisan the king sees Nehemiah's sad face, and Nehemiah, "very sore afraid," tells him the city of his fathers lies waste (Nehemiah 2:1–3). He prays to the God of heaven, asks to be sent to rebuild it, and the king gives him letters and timber, "according to the good hand of my God upon me" (Nehemiah 2:4–8). He travels with captains and horsemen, and Sanballat and Tobiah are grieved that someone has come to help Israel (Nehemiah 2:9–10). After three days in Jerusalem he views the broken walls by night (Nehemiah 2:11–16). He tells the rulers, "let us build up the wall of Jerusalem," and they answer, "Let us rise up and build" (Nehemiah 2:17–18). Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem laugh them to scorn, but Nehemiah says, "The God of heaven, he will prosper us" (Nehemiah 2:19–20).
Nehemiah 2.whereWeAre: Nehemiah prayed for Jerusalem in chapter 1. Now King Artaxerxes sends him with letters and timber, he inspects the broken walls at night, and the people agree to build. Chapter 3 lists who repaired each part of the wall.

keyFigures.name: Nehemiah
keyFigures.role: Asks the king to send him, inspects the walls, and calls the people to build.

keyFigures.name: Artaxerxes
keyFigures.role: King of Persia, who grants letters, timber, and an escort.

keyFigures.name: Sanballat the Horonite
keyFigures.role: Grieved at Nehemiah's coming; mocks the builders.

keyFigures.name: Tobiah the Ammonite
keyFigures.role: Joins Sanballat in opposing the work.

keyFigures.name: Geshem the Arabian
keyFigures.role: Laughs the builders to scorn.

keyFigures.name: The rulers of the Jews
keyFigures.role: Answer Nehemiah, "Let us rise up and build."

keyThemes.explanation: Nehemiah prays silently and then asks the king for what he needs.
Nehemiah credits God's hand for the king's favor.
Nehemiah answers scorn by trusting the God of heaven to prosper them.

Nehemiah 3.summary: Eliashib the high priest and the priests build the sheep gate and sanctify it (Nehemiah 3:1). Section by section, families, towns, goldsmiths, apothecaries, and merchants repair the wall and its gates, each "next unto" the other (Nehemiah 3:2–32). The men of Tekoa work, but "their nobles put not their necks to the work of their Lord" (Nehemiah 3:5). Shallum, ruler of half of Jerusalem, repairs his part, "he and his daughters" (Nehemiah 3:12). Many repair the wall in front of their own houses (Nehemiah 3:23, 28–30).
Nehemiah 3.whereWeAre: The people agreed to rebuild in chapter 2. This chapter goes around the city gate by gate, naming the priests, families, and workers who repaired each section. In chapter 4 their enemies mock them and plot an attack.

keyFigures.name: Eliashib
keyFigures.role: The high priest, who builds the sheep gate with the priests.

keyFigures.name: Shallum
keyFigures.role: Ruler of half of Jerusalem, who repairs his section with his daughters.

keyFigures.name: The Tekoites
keyFigures.role: Repair two sections, though their nobles refuse to work.

keyFigures.name: The builders of Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: Families, goldsmiths, apothecaries, and merchants who each repair a section.

keyThemes.explanation: Priests, rulers, craftsmen, and families all repair a section of the wall.
Many build the part of the wall in front of their own houses.
The nobles of Tekoa are remembered for not putting their necks to the work.

Nehemiah 4.summary: Sanballat mocks "these feeble Jews," and Tobiah says a fox could break down their wall (Nehemiah 4:1–3). Nehemiah prays, "Hear, O our God; for we are despised," and the wall rises to half its height, "for the people had a mind to work" (Nehemiah 4:4–6). When the enemies plot to attack, the people pray and set a watch day and night (Nehemiah 4:7–9). The workers grow tired, and Jews living near the enemies warn them ten times (Nehemiah 4:10–12). Nehemiah arms the families and tells them, "remember the Lord, which is great and terrible, and fight" (Nehemiah 4:13–14). From then on half work and half stand guard, every builder wears a sword, and a trumpet is ready to call them together (Nehemiah 4:15–23).
Nehemiah 4.whereWeAre: Chapter 3 showed the whole city at work on the wall. Now Sanballat and Tobiah mock the builders and plan to attack, so the people build with one hand and hold a weapon with the other. Chapter 5 brings trouble from inside the community.

keyFigures.name: Sanballat
keyFigures.role: Mocks "these feeble Jews" and plots an attack.

keyFigures.name: Tobiah
keyFigures.role: Jokes that a fox could break down the wall.

keyFigures.name: Nehemiah
keyFigures.role: Prays, sets a watch, and arms the builders.

keyFigures.name: The builders
keyFigures.role: Work with one hand and hold a weapon with the other.

keyThemes.explanation: The people pray to God and also set a watch day and night.
The wall rises because the people are willing to work.
Nehemiah tells them to remember the great and terrible Lord and fight for their families.

Nehemiah 5.summary: There is a great cry of the people against their brethren the Jews: in a dearth they have mortgaged their land and sold their children to pay for grain and the king's tribute (Nehemiah 5:1–5). Nehemiah is very angry and tells the nobles and rulers, "Ye exact usury, every one of his brother" (Nehemiah 5:6–9). He tells them to give back the lands and the interest, and they promise, "We will restore them" (Nehemiah 5:10–12). He shakes out his lap as a sign, and the people say "Amen" and praise the LORD (Nehemiah 5:13). For twelve years as governor, Nehemiah does not eat "the bread of the governor" and feeds 150 at his table at his own cost (Nehemiah 5:14–18). He prays, "Think upon me, my God, for good" (Nehemiah 5:19).
Nehemiah 5.whereWeAre: The builders held off their enemies in chapter 4. Now poor families cry out that richer Jews have taken their land and their children for debt, and Nehemiah makes the nobles give it back. In chapter 6 the enemies try new tricks against Nehemiah himself.

keyFigures.name: The poor of the people
keyFigures.role: Cry out that they have lost their land and children to debt.

keyFigures.name: Nehemiah
keyFigures.role: Rebukes the lenders and refuses the governor's allowance.

keyFigures.name: The nobles and rulers
keyFigures.role: Promise to give back the land and the interest.

keyFigures.name: The priests
keyFigures.role: Put the lenders under oath.

keyThemes.explanation: Nehemiah will not let the rich take their brothers' land and children.
The lenders swear before the priests to give back what they took.
Nehemiah refuses the governor's food and feeds others at his own cost.

Nehemiah 6.summary: Sanballat and Geshem ask Nehemiah four times to meet them in the plain of Ono, but he answers, "I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down" (Nehemiah 6:1–4). An open letter accuses him of planning to be king, and he replies that they invented it and prays, "O God, strengthen my hands" (Nehemiah 6:5–9). Shemaiah, hired by Tobiah and Sanballat, urges him to hide in the temple, but Nehemiah says, "Should such a man as I flee?" (Nehemiah 6:10–14). The wall is finished on the twenty-fifth day of Elul, in fifty-two days, and the nations see "that this work was wrought of our God" (Nehemiah 6:15–16). Still, nobles of Judah keep sending letters to and from Tobiah, and Tobiah sends letters to frighten Nehemiah (Nehemiah 6:17–19).
Nehemiah 6.whereWeAre: Nehemiah ended the abuse of the poor in chapter 5. Now his enemies try to lure him away, accuse him of rebellion, and frighten him into hiding in the temple, but the wall is finished in fifty-two days. Chapter 7 sets guards and turns to the people.

keyFigures.name: Nehemiah
keyFigures.role: Refuses every trap and finishes the wall.

keyFigures.name: Sanballat and Geshem
keyFigures.role: Try to lure Nehemiah to Ono and accuse him of rebellion.

keyFigures.name: Shemaiah
keyFigures.role: Son of Delaiah, hired to frighten Nehemiah into the temple.

keyFigures.name: Noadiah
keyFigures.role: A prophetess who also tries to make Nehemiah afraid.

keyFigures.name: Tobiah
keyFigures.role: Keeps writing to the nobles of Judah and sending letters to frighten Nehemiah.

keyThemes.explanation: Nehemiah will not stop his great work to meet his enemies.
He denies false charges and asks God to strengthen his hands.
He refuses to hide in the temple and break God's law to save himself.
Even the enemies see that the wall was built by God.

Nehemiah 7.summary: With the wall built and the doors set up, Nehemiah appoints porters, singers, and Levites and gives Hanani and Hananiah charge over Jerusalem (Nehemiah 7:1–2). The gates are not to be opened until the sun is hot, and the people keep watch by their houses (Nehemiah 7:3). The city is large but has few people, so God puts it in Nehemiah's heart to count the people, and he finds the register of the first return (Nehemiah 7:4–5). The register lists the families, priests, Levites, and servants who came up with Zerubbabel, 42,360 in all (Nehemiah 7:6–69). The governor, the chief fathers, and the people give gold, silver, and garments for the work, and all live in their cities (Nehemiah 7:70–73).
Nehemiah 7.whereWeAre: The wall was finished in chapter 6. Now Nehemiah puts the city under guard and finds the list of those who first came home with Zerubbabel. In chapter 8 the people gather to hear Ezra read the law.

keyFigures.name: Nehemiah
keyFigures.role: Sets guards over the city and gathers the people to be counted.

keyFigures.name: Hanani
keyFigures.role: Nehemiah's brother, given charge over Jerusalem.

keyFigures.name: Hananiah
keyFigures.role: The ruler of the palace, "a faithful man," given charge with Hanani.

keyThemes.explanation: Nehemiah gives the city to men who are faithful and fear God.
The gates are watched and opened only in full daylight.
The old register ties the people to those who first returned.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Both preserve lists of the returning exiles, although some names and figures vary.

Nehemiah 8.summary: All the people gather "as one man" at the water gate and ask Ezra to bring the book of the law of Moses (Nehemiah 8:1). Ezra reads it from a pulpit of wood from morning until midday, and the people answer, "Amen, Amen" (Nehemiah 8:2–6). The Levites read "distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading" (Nehemiah 8:7–8). When the people weep, Nehemiah and Ezra tell them, "neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Nehemiah 8:9–12). The next day the leaders find that Israel should dwell in booths at the feast of the seventh month (Nehemiah 8:13–15). The people make booths, as they had not done since the days of Joshua, and Ezra reads the law every day of the feast (Nehemiah 8:16–18).
Nehemiah 8.whereWeAre: The people had settled in their towns at the end of chapter 7. Now in the seventh month they gather at the water gate, Ezra reads the law, and their tears turn to joy as they keep the feast of booths. Chapter 9 brings a day of fasting and confession.

keyFigures.name: Ezra
keyFigures.role: The scribe who reads the law to the people from a pulpit of wood.

keyFigures.name: Nehemiah
keyFigures.role: The governor, who tells the people not to weep but to rejoice.

keyFigures.name: The Levites
keyFigures.role: Help the people understand the reading.

keyFigures.name: All the people
keyFigures.role: Listen, weep, and then keep the feast of booths with great gladness.

keyThemes.explanation: The people stand and listen to the law from morning until midday.
The Levites explain the reading so the people understand.
The people are told not to grieve, for the joy of the LORD is their strength.
They find the command about booths and keep it at once.

Nehemiah 9.summary: On the twenty-fourth day of the month the people fast in sackcloth, separate from strangers, and confess their sins (Nehemiah 9:1–3). The Levites call out, "Stand up and bless the LORD your God," and praise him as the maker of heaven and earth (Nehemiah 9:4–6). The prayer recalls God's call of Abram, the exodus, Sinai, and the manna and water in the wilderness (Nehemiah 9:7–15). When their fathers rebelled, God did not forsake them, for he is "a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful" (Nehemiah 9:16–21). God gave them the land, yet they killed the prophets, and he delivered them to their enemies and rescued them many times (Nehemiah 9:22–31). The prayer ends, "Behold, we are servants this day," and the people make a sure covenant in writing (Nehemiah 9:32–38).
Nehemiah 9.whereWeAre: The people kept the feast with great gladness in chapter 8. Now they fast in sackcloth, and the Levites lead a prayer that retells Israel's history of sin and God's mercy. It ends with a written covenant, signed in chapter 10.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Fast, confess their sins, and make a written covenant.

keyFigures.name: The Levites
keyFigures.role: Lead the people in praise and in the long prayer of confession.

keyThemes.explanation: The people fast and confess their own sins and their fathers' sins.
The prayer retells how God kept his promises from Abram to the land.
Each time Israel rebelled and cried out, God showed mercy.
Their confession leads to a written covenant.

Nehemiah 10.summary: Nehemiah the Tirshatha, the priests, the Levites, and the chief of the people seal the covenant (Nehemiah 10:1–27). The rest of the people join them in an oath "to walk in God's law, which was given by Moses" (Nehemiah 10:28–29). They promise not to give their children in marriage to the peoples of the land and not to buy on the sabbath, and to let the land rest every seventh year (Nehemiah 10:30–31). They pledge a third of a shekel a year for the temple service and cast lots for the wood offering (Nehemiah 10:32–34). They promise firstfruits, firstborn, and tithes, ending, "we will not forsake the house of our God" (Nehemiah 10:35–39).
Nehemiah 10.whereWeAre: Chapter 9 ended with a promise to make a sure covenant in writing. Now Nehemiah and the leaders seal it, and the people swear to keep God's law, the sabbath, and the support of the temple. In chapter 11 families move into Jerusalem.

keyFigures.name: Nehemiah
keyFigures.role: The Tirshatha, or governor, the first to seal the covenant.

keyFigures.name: The priests, Levites, and chief of the people
keyFigures.role: Seal the covenant by name.

keyFigures.name: The rest of the people
keyFigures.role: Swear an oath to walk in God's law.

keyThemes.explanation: Leaders put their names on the covenant, and all the people swear to keep it.
The promises cover marriage, the sabbath, debts, and offerings.
The people pledge money, wood, firstfruits, and tithes for the temple.

Nehemiah 11.summary: The rulers live in Jerusalem, and the rest of the people cast lots "to bring one of ten to dwell in Jerusalem the holy city" (Nehemiah 11:1). The people bless the men who willingly offer to live there (Nehemiah 11:2). The chapter lists the families of Judah and Benjamin who live in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:3–9). It lists the priests, Levites, porters, and singers who serve the house of God (Nehemiah 11:10–24). The others live in towns and villages of Judah, from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom, and in the towns of Benjamin (Nehemiah 11:25–36).
Nehemiah 11.whereWeAre: The people sealed their covenant in chapter 10. Now one in ten is chosen by lot to live in Jerusalem, and the chapter lists the families of the city and the towns around it. Chapter 12 lists the priests and Levites and dedicates the wall.

keyFigures.name: The rulers of the people
keyFigures.role: Already live in Jerusalem.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Cast lots so one in ten will live in Jerusalem.

keyFigures.name: The volunteers
keyFigures.role: Willingly offer to live in the city and are blessed for it.

keyThemes.explanation: Some leave their farms to make Jerusalem strong.
Priests, Levites, and singers live where the temple stands.
Families fill the towns of Judah and Benjamin again.

Nehemiah 12.summary: The chapter lists the priests and Levites who came up with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, and their families down to the days of Nehemiah and Ezra (Nehemiah 12:1–26). For the dedication of the wall the Levites are brought to Jerusalem, and the priests and Levites purify themselves, the people, the gates, and the wall (Nehemiah 12:27–30). Nehemiah sets two great companies of singers on the wall, one led by Ezra the scribe, and they go around in opposite directions to the house of God (Nehemiah 12:31–42). They offer great sacrifices, "so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off" (Nehemiah 12:43). Men are put over the storerooms, and Judah gladly gives the portions for the priests, Levites, singers, and porters (Nehemiah 12:44–47).
Nehemiah 12.whereWeAre: Chapter 11 filled Jerusalem with people. Now the priests and Levites are listed, and two great companies march on the wall in thanks until "the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off" (Nehemiah 12:43). In chapter 13 Nehemiah returns to find the covenant broken.

keyFigures.name: Nehemiah
keyFigures.role: Brings the princes onto the wall and leads one company.

keyFigures.name: Ezra
keyFigures.role: The scribe who goes before the first company.

keyFigures.name: The priests and Levites
keyFigures.role: Purify the people and the wall and lead the thanksgiving.

keyFigures.name: The singers
keyFigures.role: Sing loudly in two great companies on the wall.

keyThemes.explanation: Two great companies give thanks as they walk on the wall.
The whole city's joy is heard far away.
The priests and Levites purify themselves and the people first.
Judah gladly supports those who serve in the temple.

Nehemiah 13.summary: The people read that no Ammonite or Moabite may enter the congregation, and they separate the mixed multitude from Israel (Nehemiah 13:1–3). While Nehemiah is away with the king, Eliashib gives Tobiah a great chamber in the temple, and on his return Nehemiah throws out Tobiah's goods (Nehemiah 13:4–9). He finds the Levites unpaid and gone to their fields, asks, "Why is the house of God forsaken?" and brings them back (Nehemiah 13:10–14). He sees work and trade on the sabbath, rebukes the nobles, and shuts the gates from evening until the sabbath is over (Nehemiah 13:15–22). He finds men married to women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab, makes them swear, and chases away a grandson of Eliashib who married Sanballat's daughter (Nehemiah 13:23–29). He cleanses the priests and Levites and ends, "Remember me, O my God, for good" (Nehemiah 13:30–31).
Nehemiah 13.whereWeAre: Chapter 12 ended in joy and faithful giving. Now, after Nehemiah's time away at the king's court, he finds Tobiah living in the temple, the Levites unpaid, the sabbath broken, and mixed marriages again. Esther tells another story of God's people in Persia, set earlier at Shushan.

keyFigures.name: Nehemiah
keyFigures.role: Returns to Jerusalem and sets right what had gone wrong.

keyFigures.name: Eliashib

keyFigures.name: Tobiah
keyFigures.role: Nehemiah's old enemy, thrown out of the temple chamber.

keyFigures.name: The nobles of Judah
keyFigures.role: Rebuked for allowing trade on the sabbath.

keyFigures.name: The men of Tyre
keyFigures.role: Sell fish and goods in Jerusalem on the sabbath.

keyFigures.name: A son of Joiada
keyFigures.role: Grandson of Eliashib and son-in-law of Sanballat, chased away by Nehemiah.

keyThemes.explanation: Soon after the covenant, the people break the very things they promised.
Nehemiah shuts the gates to stop trade on the holy day.
Nehemiah reminds them that foreign wives led even Solomon into sin.
Nehemiah asks God again and again to remember him for good.
